subject: Agriculture
title: Nitrogen-Fixing Bacteria
description: A micro-lesson that makes Nitrogen-Fixing Bacteria usable.

hook.text: Air is 78% nitrogen, but plants can't use it. It's locked in a form they can't absorb.

buildup.text: Rhizobium bacteria live in nodules on legume roots and convert atmospheric nitrogen into plant-usable ammonia.

discovery.text: This natural nitrogen fixation is why farmers rotate crops with legumes—clover, beans, and alfalfa enrich the soil.

twist.text: Adding synthetic nitrogen fertilizer suppresses these bacteria. Why fix nitrogen for free when it's already abundant?

climax.text: Organic farms rely heavily on biological fixation. It's slower but sustainable and costs nothing.

punchline.text: Bacteria do for free what factories do with fossil fuels.

quiz.question: How do Rhizobium bacteria help legume plants?
options: They convert atmospheric nitrogen into usable ammonia
They store water in root nodules

details.summary: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen gas into plant-available ammonium through a process that powers natural soil fertility. Rhizobia bacteria in legume root nodules and free-living bacteria like Azotobacter provide free nitrogen that reduces fertilizer dependence.
details.whyItMatters: Biological nitrogen fixation supplies an estimated 100-200 million tons of nitrogen to ecosystems annually—more than all synthetic fertilizer production.
takeaways: Rhizobia bacteria in legume root nodules fix 50-300 kg of nitrogen per hectare per year
Biological fixation provides more nitrogen to global ecosystems than all fertilizer factories
The legume-Rhizobium symbiosis is the foundation of crop rotation fertility management

faq.question: How do nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into plant food?
faq.answer: Rhizobia bacteria infect legume roots and form nodules where the enzyme nitrogenase converts N2 gas into ammonium (NH4+). The plant provides sugars and a low-oxygen environment the enzyme needs. The ammonium is used by the plant and released to soil when roots decompose.

faq.question: Why are legumes so important in crop rotation systems?
faq.answer: Legumes like soybeans, clover, and beans host Rhizobium bacteria that fix 50-300 kg of nitrogen per hectare. When the legume crop is terminated, this nitrogen becomes available to the following crop, reducing or eliminating the need for synthetic nitrogen fertilizer.
